claims.text: Conventionally cast tungsten alloys exhibit a random crystallographic texture.
Directional solidification with controlled cooling rates can produce a predominant crystallographic texture in tungsten alloys.
The engineered texture aligns the primary slip systems with the loading direction.
The engineered crystallographic texture activates preferential slip systems.
A favorable crystallographic texture reduces the critical resolved shear stress on the primary slip systems.
Reduced critical resolved shear stress enhances dislocation motion.
Enhanced dislocation motion promotes uniform high-temperature plastic flow.
Engineered texture will lower the yield stress relative to a conventionally cast, randomly textured baseline.
Engineered texture will increase total plastic strain relative to the baseline.
Engineered texture will improve toughness relative to the baseline.
The hypothesized behavior applies at approximately 1200°C under uniaxial tension in directionally solidified tungsten alloys.
The sensitivity of the mechanism to alloy composition and processing variations has not been definitively established.
A controlled test will compare directionally solidified, textured specimens with conventionally cast, randomly textured specimens under the same tensile-test environment.
EBSD will be used to verify the intended crystallographic texture.
TEM will be used to evaluate dislocation structures and activity.
The hypothesis will be falsified if textured specimens show no statistically significant reduction in yield stress together with increased plastic strain and improved toughness.

contradictions.description: The conditions state that all specimens experience identical processing except for texture, but the proposed groups are produced by different processing routes—directional solidification versus conventional casting—and the baseline additionally has 'traditionally processed microstructures.' Thus processing route and potentially microstructure are confounded with texture.
